title: Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RLon Agentic Coding Tasks

paper.title: Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks
paper.abstract: Abstract Coding agents often fail in the last mile: they build most of a feature but drop a requirement, test only the cases their implementation already handles, break behavior that was supposed to stay intact, or validate against an unchecked assumption. We ask whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks closes this gap, and whether what the agent learns transfers beyond the training distribution. We post-train Kimi K2.7 Code, a 1T-parameter (32B active) open-weight mixture-of-experts model, with RL alone on 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and by pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The reward is the fraction of target checks passed and drops to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails. One epoch of GSPO on a rank-32 LoRA adapter improves pass@1 on each of the six external benchmarks we evaluated, across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1 → \rightarrow 64.8), DeepSWE (31.0 → \rightarrow 43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4 → \rightarrow 82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4 → \rightarrow 12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0 → \rightarrow 7.6), and SWE-Marathon (5.0 → \rightarrow 25.0). Pooled over the five independent task sets (Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3), the improvement is significant ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), and it remains significant on the three sets released after the training data was collected ( p = 0.004 p=0.004 ); the model also improves under both harnesses never used in training. Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 are 24–35% shorter in agent steps. The base model’s failed DeepSWE runs are mostly near-misses, and on the tasks the trained model newly solves, paired trajectories show it avoiding each of the four failure modes above.

The base model’s failed DeepSWE runs are mostly near-misses, and on the tasks the trained model newly solves, paired trajectories show it avoiding each of the four failure modes above. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is now a standard stage in training coding agents [ DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ] . The usual evidence that a run worked is a higher score on a benchmark whose format the training data shares. That leaves two questions open. What did the model learn: domain knowledge, or something more general about carrying a task to completion? And does the improvement survive a change of benchmark, agent harness, and horizon? An agent that has absorbed one benchmark’s conventions is worth less than one that has learned to finish realistic work. Figure 1: Pass@1 on six external benchmarks before and after RL on 1,700 expert-built coding tasks, grouped by task format, with SWE-Marathon’s multi-hour builds shown separately. Bold numbers are gains in percentage points. Harnesses are in italics, in bold for the two not used in training. Hatched baselines are publicly reported scores for the same checkpoint and harness (DeepSWE: benchmark leaderboard; Terminal-Bench 2.1: Artificial Analysis); the others are in-house runs. Asterisks mark benchmarks released after the training data was collected; Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3. We study both questions with one training run and six external benchmarks. We post-train Kimi K2.7 Code [ Moonshot AI, 2026 ] with RL alone on 1,700 expert-built agentic coding tasks from two families (§ 3 ). Each of the 1,000 repository tasks pairs a real repository at a pinned commit with a change request; hidden fail-to-pass tests grade the change, and pass-to-pass tests guard existing behavior. Each of the 700 terminal tasks pairs a working environment with a deliverable graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The recipe is deliberately simple, so that what the run tests is the tasks and their reward: Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] on a rank-32 LoRA adapter [ Hu et al., 2022 ] , no supervised warm-up, no KL penalty, and a partial-credit reward, the fraction of satisfied checks, that drops to zero whenever a pass-to-pass test regresses (§ 4 ). We compare the base and trained models on SWE-Bench Pro, DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1, 3, and 4, and SWE-Marathon, fixing one harness per benchmark, three harnesses in all (§ 5 ). The six cover both training formats, new task sources and domains, and a horizon absent from training: SWE-Marathon’s multi-hour builds. Four were released after the training data was collected. The trained model improves on all six (§ 6 ; Figure 1 ), by 4.7 to 20.0 percentage points (pp), including under both harnesses never used in training: Claude Code on SWE-Marathon (1 to 5 of 20 tasks) and Terminus 2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (+14.6 pp over its public baseline). Because Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3, the six benchmarks form five independent task sets; pooled over them, the improvement is significant ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), and it remains significant on the three sets released after the training data was collected ( p = 0.004 p=0.004 ). The trained model also takes fewer agent steps: the median falls from 150 to 98 on DeepSWE and from 102 to 78 on Terminal-Bench 3. To see what changed, we paired base and trained trajectories on the same tasks (§ 7 ). The base model’s DeepSWE failures are mostly near-misses: the median failed run still passes 86% of its target tests, and 84% of failed runs keep every pass-to-pass test. In the pairs we read, all from tasks the trained model newly solves, the base model’s failures recur in four modes that follow a standard engineering loop: lost requirements (understand), narrow testing (test), silent regressions (maintain), and weak ground truth (verify). On the same tasks, the trained model implements the entire specification, derives its tests from the requirement instead of from its own implementation, tracks what must keep working, and builds its own ground truth when none is provided. Each behavior is one the training tasks and reward favor. The evidence points to what transfers: not domain knowledge, which the base model largely had, but a way of finishing work. Contributions. 1. Transfer from a small expert-built RL dataset: one epoch on 1,700 tasks improves pass@1 on all six external benchmarks we evaluated, under three harnesses, including four released after the data was collected and one whose multi-hour horizon has no counterpart in training (§ 6 ). 2. A paired trajectory analysis showing that the base model’s DeepSWE failures are mostly last-mile near-misses and that, on tasks the trained model newly solves, the base model’s failures recur in four modes that the trained model avoids (§ 7 ). 3. A partial-credit reward gated on regressions, with an account that links each behavior change to a property of the training tasks and reward (§§ 3 – 4 , § 7 ). 2 Related Work RL for software-engineering agents. RLVR was named and established on mathematics and instruction following [ Lambert et al., 2025 ] ; DeepSeek-R1 scaled rule-based rewards, optimized with GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] , to mathematics and short-form code [ DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ] , and RL has since moved to long-horizon agentic software engineering. SWE-RL [ Wei et al., 2025 ] learns from software-evolution data with a rule-based patch-similarity reward; SWE-Gym [ Pan et al., 2025 ] , SWE-smith [ Yang et al., 2025 ] , and R2E-Gym [ Jain et al., 2025 ] build executable training environments from real repositories at scale; DeepSWE-Preview [ Luo et al., 2025 ] , an agent unrelated to the DeepSWE benchmark, trains with RL alone in such environments; SkyRL [ Cao et al., 2025 ] provides an RL pipeline for long-horizon agents; and frontier open models such as Kimi K2 [ Kimi Team et al., 2025 ] combine large-scale agentic data synthesis with RL. These efforts mostly mine or synthesize tasks at scale and evaluate on SWE-bench-style benchmarks [ Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Chowdhury et al., 2024 ] whose format matches the training environments. We train on a small set of expert-built tasks whose specifications enumerate individually gradable requirements, with partial credit gated on regressions, and measure transfer across benchmarks, harnesses, and horizons. Benchmarks for agentic coding. SWE-bench [ Jimenez et al., 2024 ] and its human-validated subset [ Chowdhury et al., 2024 ] made issue resolution on real repositories the standard task; SWE-Bench Pro [ Deng et al., 2026 ] raises difficulty with long-horizon, multi-file, human-verified problems. Terminal-Bench [ Merrill et al., 2026 ] evaluates agents on hard tasks in containerized command-line environments and, through the Harbor framework [ Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ] , has become a continuously versioned benchmark (versions 2.0, 2.1, 3, and 4) [ Terminal-Bench Team, 2026 ; Marten et al., 2026 ; Marten, 2026 ] . DeepSWE [ Huang et al., 2026 ] asks for original features in existing repositories, and SWE-Marathon [ Desai et al., 2026 ] for complete systems over multi-hour horizons. Scores on all of these depend on the agent harness [ Merrill et al., 2026 ; Desai et al., 2026 ] , which fixes the tools, prompts, and control loop the model operates in. Common harnesses include SWE-agent and mini-swe-agent [ Yang et al., 2024 ; Lieret and Jimenez, 2025 ] , OpenHands [ Wang et al., 2025 ] , Terminus 2 [ Merrill et al., 2026 ] , and commercial CLIs such as Claude Code [ Anthropic, 2025 ] . Partial-credit and rubric-based rewards. Rewards proportional to the fraction of unit tests passed are established in code RL [ Liu et al., 2023 ] . Rubric-based rewards have been used to train instruction following [ He et al., 2026 ; Mehta et al., 2026a ] and open-ended reasoning [ Gunjal et al., 2026 ] ; Mehta et al. [2026a] reward the fraction of expert-written criteria satisfied. Proxy rewards can be gamed [ Skalse et al., 2022 ] , and partial credit opens a specific trade: satisfying new checks at the expense of existing behavior. Our reward keeps partial credit on the requested behavior and removes that trade with a gate that assigns zero reward whenever a pass-to-pass test fails. Transfer from post-training. Chu et al. [2025] find that RL generalizes to unseen rule and visual variants where supervised fine-tuning memorizes; Huan et al. [2026] find that RL on mathematics transfers to other domains better than supervised fine-tuning on the same problems; Yue et al. [2025] argue that much of RLVR’s pass@1 gain on reasoning tasks comes from concentrating probability on solutions the base model could already sample. Prior work from our group reports transfer across task distributions: post-training on long-horizon multi-tool office work, with no software-engineering tasks, produced gains on five external evaluations, including SWE-Bench Pro from 20.5% to 26.3% [ Mehta et al., 2026c ; Ritchie et al., 2026 ] ; single-turn constraint-following training produced its largest gains on multi-turn dimensions, led by +22.1 pp on MultiChallenge instruction retention [ Mehta et al., 2026a ; Deshpande et al., 2025 ] ; and training on an enterprise simulation improved out-of-distribution pass rates [ Mehta et al., 2026b ] . Here training and evaluation are both coding, but the benchmarks, harnesses, and horizons differ. 3 Training Data The training set consists of 1,700 tasks from Surge AI’s expert-built agentic coding collections, in the two formats most common in agentic coding evaluation. Every task pairs a specification the agent sees with hidden checks of the requested behavior. 3.1 Two task families Repository tasks (1,000).
